[b]EDF first class Paratrooper Jacob Hueves[/b]

The news came down hard this morning. The 3rd Paratrooper Division is deploying to Sal-Baliz. No more training drills, no more waitingwere going in for real.

The barracks are a mess of movement, the sound of duffel bags being slammed shut, zippers buzzing, weapons being checked and rechecked. I sit on my bunk, rolling up my gear, forcing my hands to stay steady. Its not fearno, weve trained for thisbut theres a weight to knowing that in just hours, Ill be boarding that transport with my unit, heading straight into hostile territory.

Sergeant ODell barks orders from down the hall. You got two hours! Pack smart, pack fast! If youre carrying extra, youre carrying it for the enemy! His voice is sharp, but I can tell its for show. Even he knows this is different. We all do.

I toss in my fatigues, extra rations, ammo, a few personal effects. A photo of my mother. A letter from my little brother, barely legible with his messy handwriting. I fold it carefully and slide it into my chest pocket.

The mess hall is louder than usual. Guys joking, talking big, trying to push back the reality of whats coming. I shake hands, clap backs, exchange the usual see you on the other side. But theres an undercurrent, a sense that not all of us might.

Before we leave, I make the call. My mother picks up after the first ring. She knows. I dont even have to say it. She tells me shes proud, that shell be waiting. I keep it short. No room for drawn-out goodbyes.

Then its time. Boots on, rifle slung, last-minute checks. The transport hums on the tarmac, the engines waiting. This is it. Sal-Baliz wont know what hit them.

We jump soon.

[quote=tulunid;58775231]and thats not to forget what happened at the presentation. I had made tons of notes that I needed to use for the big day, and when that day came, I had lost all of them! I looked for those notes everywhere, all morning, until eventually, one of the cleaners admitted they had accidentally thrown it away thinking it was rubbish. I was mad, until your Ummi came to me, smiling and holding something. I know how silly you can be sometimes, she told me, so I made sure to put all your notes into a PowerPoint so you dont lose any of them! And by Allah I tell you my child, that PowerPoint was one thousand times better than any notes I had made. Your Ummi was always so good with technology. The child giggled. Can you tell me more about her? The father laughed. Not now, its time to sleep. Auntie* Amina will tuck you in, okay? The child nodded. Sweet dreams, my child. 

The man left the room, and took a right at the corridor to the room at the far end. He opened the door to his own bedroom, not as large as what might be expected for a king, but grandeur nonetheless. He set out a prayer mat and began to pray, once again cursing himself for forgetting to do so with the congregation. The Imam would surely chastise him the next time he saw him, and he would feel regretful. 

Once he finished prayers, he walked out of the room, onto the adjoining balcony. And below the balcony, a full view of Quhayba itself. Immediately in front of him, the walls of the old citadel, once an impenetrable fortress, and although its walls would not hold out against even the flimsiest of improvised explosives, it still granted him the feeling of security, of safety. Within its walls, guards strapped with assault rifles talked with the locals in the areas, and advising the tourists on where to go. Beyond the walls, Quhaybas city landscape spread out in front of him, flanked by hills on one side and the sea on the other. The smell of the salt of the sea filled his nose, and the gentle waves somehow managed to remain heard in the backdrop of the citys noise. He could almost hear the voices of taxi drivers overcharging tourists, of the Grand Bazaar with its variety of Quhayban street food. He could see the tourist sector, still buzzing with people from all over the world. He was told that the contentment provided by Jannah, heaven, was unimaginable, but for him, this was close. Perhaps if his beloved was still alive, it would have been.

And those were his last thoughts, Jannah and his wife. The last thing he felt was a sharp push from behind, sending the ruler and father off the balcony and to his death.

Abu Tamim Ahmad bin Tulun Al-Karim was dead.

Note: Auntie Amina is not the actual aunt of the child, just a respectful term used to refer to an older woman.[/quote]

TLDR before this point: Ahmed ibn Uthman ibn Tulun has been thrown out of his balcony and killed.

[spoiler=Jafar ibn Uthman ibn Tulun]
Jafar was stood in the first row ready for the funeral prayer to start. To his left and right, brothers, uncles, cousins and nephews. Immediately next to him, a child who was not crying, but with tears all over his face. In front of him, a half brother, supposedly the most righteous man in the family who was allocated to lead the prayer.

Allahu Akbar

In an instant, quiet whispers around the mosque courtyard turned to utter silence. Apparently his brother had told the Imam that he wished to be buried here, a simple gravestone to mark the burial site. He didnt know about this, but it did sound like him.

And as even the streets around the mosque quietened down, seemingly out of respect, Jafar began to remember. Jafar, you can come in now! It was his father, calling him into his parents bedroom. His mother lay in the bed, all around her medical equipment and nurses. She beamed at him, too weak to speak but signalling him over. Do you want to hold him? Jafar nodded eagerly, and one of the nurses took Ahmed out of her hands and into his lap.

Allah Akbar.

His father had championed a tradition of going out into the desert with his family at least once a year. The first one after his mothers death, Jafar hadnt expected him to keep it up. But he had, and this year he had invited the entire extended family too. And it was on a night during that trip where he had named his successor. With the passing of my dear Khadijah the inevitable fate has given us yet another reminder that none of us can escape it. As such, it is necessary we prepare for it. And for me, this involves ensuring the safety of our nation and the succession. After consulting the Ulema, the governors and my beloved before she passed away, I have made a decision. Ahmed will lead the family and the country after my death. Should he die before me, Jafar will take his place, and should he take power, he is free to choose his own successor.

One by one, all the family members in the little tent in the desert stood up to the give the bait for Ahmed. He heard the murmurs, and when their eyes full of pity fell upon him, he stared right back, unfazed.

Allahu Akbar

The moon, its impressive how bright it shines from so far away. Jafar had not heard his fathers approach, drowned by the chatter from the tent and muffled by the sands of the desert. He put his hand up before Jafar could say anything. I know youre angry. I would be too. You are more than capable, you have experience, youre well known and respected, more important than all, you are the eldest son! And yet, despite it all, you are not chosen. Jafar may have been in his 20s, but he still dared not to speak back to his father. In short, you are everything which made me successful. And that is exactly why you cannot be my successor. Jafar looked at his father, puzzled. His father barely smiled, and he never dared to show weakness, not in any normal conditions.

But these were far from normal conditions.

Your capability makes you a realist, not a dreamer. Your experience has forced you to deal with horrible people, and the bias towards them in your rule will show. You may think youre respected, but fear and respect look very similar. By the will of Allah, I have had a successful reign, and unless Allah Himself intervenes, you will too. But this country deserves more. It deserves not a capable leader, but a caring one. Not someone whose mind is in the right place, but someone whose heart is. Do you understand, Jafar? Jafar nodded, not really understanding. Your brother will need you though. He will need someone who can see through the tricks of the courtiers, someone who understands the nuances of diplomacy, a guide and a friend. Tulun founded our dynasty, but it was his brother Aleddin who was by his side every step of the way. Will you be Ahmeds Aleddin, my son?

Not barely a year into Ahmeds rule, and a mutual agreement was made to transfer Jafar to the governorship of Isqandara. For the good of our people, Ahmed had said, and Jafar had agreed. Jafar was always a phone call away, and Ahmed did call often. But every call was asking for advice. Every call was about politics. Neither brother was hostile to the other, but they both knew. Their brotherhood was undoubtedly dead.

Assalamu Alaykum Wa Rahmatullah

The prayer ended, and Jafar turned his head to the left. The child by his side had burst into tears. The only child of his own brother. A child whose name he could not even remember.
[/spoiler]
